tactics.name: Reconnaissance
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gather information they can use to plan future operations.

tactics.name: Resource Development
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to establish resources they can use to support operations.

tactics.name: Initial Access
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to get into your network.

tactics.name: Execution
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to run malicious code or instructions on a system.

tactics.name: Persistence
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to maintain their foothold.

tactics.name: Privilege Escalation
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gain higher-level permissions.

tactics.name: Stealth
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to hide and conceal their actions, appearing as normal behavior.

tactics.name: Defense Impairment
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to break security mechanisms, pipelines, and tooling so defenders can’t see or trust what’s happening.

tactics.name: Credential Access
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to steal account names and passwords.

tactics.name: Discovery
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to figure out your environment.

tactics.name: Lateral Movement
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to move through your environment.

tactics.name: Collection
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gather data of interest to their goal.

tactics.name: Command and Control
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to communicate with compromised systems to control them.

tactics.name: Exfiltration
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to steal data.

tactics.name: Impact
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to manipulate, interrupt, or destroy your systems and data.

techniques.name: Data Obfuscation
techniques.description: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

techniques.name: Junk Data
techniques.description: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.description: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

techniques.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
techniques.description: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password.

techniques.name: LSASS Memory
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

techniques.name: Security Account Manager
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored.

techniques.name: NTDS
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights.

techniques.name: LSA Secrets
techniques.description: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.

techniques.name: Cached Domain Credentials
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

techniques.name: DCSync
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

techniques.name: Proc Filesystem
techniques.description: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or `/proc`. The proc filesystem is a pseudo-filesystem used as an interface to kernel data structures for Linux based systems managing virtual memory.

techniques.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking.

techniques.name: Data from Local System
techniques.description: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

techniques.name: Direct Volume Access
techniques.description: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring.

techniques.name: System Service Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services.

techniques.name: Fallback Channels
techniques.description: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

techniques.name: Application Window Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

techniques.name: Query Registry
techniques.description: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

techniques.name: Rootkit
techniques.description: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components.

techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems.

techniques.name: Internet Connection Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Wi-Fi Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems.

techniques.name: Remote System Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system.

techniques.name: Automated Exfiltration
techniques.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

techniques.name: Traffic Duplication
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure.

techniques.name: Remote Services
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).

techniques.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB).

techniques.name: Distributed Component Object Model
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM).

techniques.name: SSH
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH).

techniques.name: VNC
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

techniques.name: Windows Remote Management
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

techniques.name: Cloud Services
techniques.description: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities.

techniques.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods.

techniques.name: Data from Removable Media
techniques.description: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

techniques.name: Binary Padding
techniques.description: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware.

techniques.name: Software Packing
techniques.description: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.

techniques.name: Steganography
techniques.description: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information.

techniques.name: Compile After Delivery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

techniques.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
techniques.description: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.

techniques.name: HTML Smuggling
techniques.description: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files.

techniques.name: Dynamic API Resolution
techniques.description: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis.

techniques.name: Stripped Payloads
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information.

techniques.name: Embedded Payloads
techniques.description: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses.

techniques.name: Command Obfuscation
techniques.description: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection.

techniques.name: Fileless Storage
techniques.description: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses.

techniques.name: LNK Icon Smuggling
techniques.description: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files.

techniques.name: Encrypted/Encoded File
techniques.description: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection.

techniques.name: Polymorphic Code
techniques.description: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection.

techniques.name: Compression
techniques.description: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files.

techniques.name: Junk Code Insertion
techniques.description: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware’s functionality.

techniques.name: SVG Smuggling
techniques.description: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files.

techniques.name: Invisible Unicode
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text.

techniques.name: Scheduled Transfer
techniques.description: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals.

techniques.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
techniques.description: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds.

techniques.name: System Owner/User Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

techniques.name: Masquerading
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

techniques.name: Invalid Code Signature
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

techniques.name: Right-to-Left Override
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

techniques.name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
techniques.description: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

techniques.name: Masquerade Task or Service
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign.

techniques.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
techniques.description: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them.

techniques.name: Space after Filename
techniques.description: Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file.

techniques.name: Double File Extension
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type.

techniques.name: Masquerade File Type
techniques.description: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents.

techniques.name: Break Process Trees
techniques.description: An adversary may attempt to evade process tree-based analysis by modifying executed malware's parent process ID (PPID).

techniques.name: Masquerade Account Name
techniques.description: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign.

techniques.name: Overwrite Process Arguments
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process.

techniques.name: Browser Fingerprint
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.

techniques.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
techniques.description: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Logon Script (Windows)
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Login Hook
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon.

techniques.name: Network Logon Script
techniques.description: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: RC Scripts
techniques.description: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system’s startup.

techniques.name: Startup Items
techniques.description: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence.

techniques.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
techniques.description: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

techniques.name: Network Sniffing
techniques.description: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Network Service Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: System Network Connections Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

techniques.name: Exfiltration over USB
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: At
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Cron
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the cron utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Systemd Timers
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse systemd timers to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Container Orchestration Job
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality provided by container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes to schedule deployment of containers configured to execute malicious code.

techniques.name: Process Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Portable Executable Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Thread Execution Hijacking
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Asynchronous Procedure Call
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Thread Local Storage
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Ptrace System Calls
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via ptrace (process trace) system calls in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Proc Memory
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the /proc filesystem in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Extra Window Memory Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Process Hollowing
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses.

techniques.name: Process Doppelgänging
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via process doppelgänging in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: VDSO Hijacking
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via VDSO hijacking in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: ListPlanting
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse list-view controls to inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Input Capture
techniques.description: Adversaries may use methods of capturing user input to obtain credentials or collect information.

techniques.name: Keylogging
techniques.description: Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them.

techniques.name: GUI Input Capture
techniques.description: Adversaries may mimic common operating system GUI components to prompt users for credentials with a seemingly legitimate prompt.

techniques.name: Web Portal Capture
techniques.description: Adversaries may install code on externally facing portals, such as a VPN login page, to capture and transmit credentials of users who attempt to log into the service.

techniques.name: Credential API Hooking
techniques.description: Adversaries may hook into Windows application programming interface (API) functions and Linux system functions to collect user credentials.

techniques.name: Process Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries.

techniques.name: PowerShell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution.

techniques.name: AppleScript
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse AppleScript for execution.

techniques.name: Windows Command Shell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution.

techniques.name: Unix Shell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Unix shell commands and scripts for execution.

techniques.name: Visual Basic
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Visual Basic (VB) for execution.

techniques.name: Python
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Python commands and scripts for execution.

techniques.name: JavaScript
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution.

techniques.name: Network Device CLI
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse scripting or built-in command line interpreters (CLI) on network devices to execute malicious command and payloads.

techniques.name: Cloud API
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse cloud APIs to execute malicious commands.

techniques.name: AutoHotKey & AutoIT
techniques.description: Adversaries may execute commands and perform malicious tasks using AutoIT and AutoHotKey automation scripts.

techniques.name: Lua
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Lua commands and scripts for execution.

techniques.name: Hypervisor CLI
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse hypervisor command line interpreters (CLIs) to execute malicious commands.

techniques.name: Container CLI/API
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse built-in CLI tools or API calls to execute malicious commands in containerized environments.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
techniques.description: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Permission Groups Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings.

techniques.name: Local Groups
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to find local system groups and permission settings.

techniques.name: Domain Groups
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to find domain-level groups and permission settings.

techniques.name: Cloud Groups
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to find cloud groups and permission settings.

techniques.name: Indicator Removal
techniques.description: Adversaries may selectively delete or modify artifacts generated to reduce indications of their presence and blend in with legitimate activity.

techniques.name: Clear Command History
techniques.description: In addition to clearing system logs, an adversary may clear the command history of a compromised account to conceal the actions undertaken during an intrusion.

techniques.name: File Deletion
techniques.description: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity.

techniques.name: Network Share Connection Removal
techniques.description: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation.

techniques.name: Timestomp
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify file time attributes to hide new files or changes to existing files.

techniques.name: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
techniques.description: Adversaries may clear or remove evidence of malicious network connections in order to clean up traces of their operations.

techniques.name: Clear Mailbox Data
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify mail and mail application data to remove evidence of their activity.

techniques.name: Clear Persistence
techniques.description: Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity.

techniques.name: Relocate Malware
techniques.description: Once a payload is delivered, adversaries may reproduce copies of the same malware on the victim system to remove evidence of their presence and/or avoid defenses.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using OSI application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: Web Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: File Transfer Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with transferring files to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: Mail Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: DNS
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: Publish/Subscribe Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using publish/subscribe (pub/sub) application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

techniques.name: Software Deployment Tools
techniques.description: Adversaries may gain access to and use centralized software suites installed within an enterprise to execute commands and move laterally through the network.

techniques.name: Data Staged
techniques.description: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory prior to Exfiltration.

techniques.name: Local Data Staging
techniques.description: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory on the local system prior to Exfiltration.

techniques.name: Remote Data Staging
techniques.description: Adversaries may stage data collected from multiple systems in a central location or directory on one system prior to Exfiltration.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Default Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a default account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Domain Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a domain account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Local Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a local account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Cloud Accounts
techniques.description: Valid accounts in cloud environments may allow adversaries to perform actions to achieve Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Taint Shared Content
techniques.description: Adversaries may deliver payloads to remote systems by adding content to shared storage locations, such as network drives or internal code repositories.

techniques.name: System Information Discovery
techniques.description: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture.

techniques.name: File and Directory Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system.

techniques.name: Account Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of valid accounts, usernames, or email addresses on a system or within a compromised environment.

techniques.name: Local Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of local system accounts.

techniques.name: Domain Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of domain accounts.

techniques.name: Email Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of email addresses and accounts.

techniques.name: Cloud Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of cloud accounts.

techniques.name: Proxy
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a connection proxy to direct network traffic between systems or act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

techniques.name: Internal Proxy
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an internal proxy to direct command and control traffic between two or more systems in a compromised environment.

techniques.name: External Proxy
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an external proxy to act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

techniques.name: Multi-hop Proxy
techniques.description: Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to disguise the source of malicious traffic.

techniques.name: Domain Fronting
techniques.description: Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTTPS. Domain fronting involves using different domain names in the SNI field of the TLS header and the Host field of the HTTP header.

techniques.name: Replication Through Removable Media
techniques.description: Adversaries may move onto systems, possibly those on disconnected or air-gapped networks, by copying malware to removable media and taking advantage of Autorun features when the media is inserted into a system and executes.

techniques.name: Communication Through Removable Media
techniques.description: Adversaries can perform command and control between compromised hosts on potentially disconnected networks using removable media to transfer commands from system to system.

techniques.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an OSI non-application layer protocol for communication between host and C2 server or among infected hosts within a network.

techniques.name: Account Manipulation
techniques.description: Adversaries may manipulate accounts to maintain and/or elevate access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Additional Cloud Credentials
techniques.description: Adversaries may add adversary-controlled credentials to a cloud account to maintain persistent access to victim accounts and instances within the environment.

techniques.name: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
techniques.description: Adversaries may grant additional permission levels to maintain persistent access to an adversary-controlled email account.

techniques.name: Additional Cloud Roles
techniques.description: An adversary may add additional roles or permissions to an adversary-controlled cloud account to maintain persistent access to a tenant.

techniques.name: SSH Authorized Keys
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify the SSH authorized_keys file to maintain persistence on a victim host.

techniques.name: Device Registration
techniques.description: Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account.

techniques.name: Additional Container Cluster Roles
techniques.description: An adversary may add additional roles or permissions to an adversary-controlled user or service account to maintain persistent access to a container orchestration system.

techniques.name: Additional Local or Domain Groups
techniques.description: An adversary may add additional local or domain groups to an adversary-controlled account to maintain persistent access to a system or domain.

techniques.name: Web Service
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for relaying data to/from a compromised system.

techniques.name: Dead Drop Resolver
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to host information that points to additional command and control (C2) infrastructure.

techniques.name: Bidirectional Communication
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel.

techniques.name: One-Way Communication
techniques.description: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to a compromised system without receiving return output over the Web service channel.

techniques.name: Multi-Stage Channels
techniques.description: Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions.

techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
techniques.description: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment.

techniques.name: Native API
techniques.description: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors.

techniques.name: Brute Force
techniques.description: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.

techniques.name: Password Guessing
techniques.description: Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts.

techniques.name: Password Cracking
techniques.description: Adversaries may use password cracking to attempt to recover usable credentials, such as plaintext passwords, when credential material such as password hashes are obtained.

techniques.name: Password Spraying
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to attempt to acquire valid account credentials.

techniques.name: Credential Stuffing
techniques.description: Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap.

techniques.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
techniques.description: Adversaries may target multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms, (i.e., smart cards, token generators, etc.) to gain access to credentials that can be used to access systems, services, and network resources.

techniques.name: Modify Registry
techniques.description: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution.

techniques.name: Screen Capture
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to take screen captures of the desktop to gather information over the course of an operation.

techniques.name: Email Collection
techniques.description: Adversaries may target user email to collect sensitive information.

techniques.name: Local Email Collection
techniques.description: Adversaries may target user email on local systems to collect sensitive information.

techniques.name: Remote Email Collection
techniques.description: Adversaries may target an Exchange server, Office 365, or Google Workspace to collect sensitive information.

techniques.name: Email Forwarding Rule
techniques.description: Adversaries may setup email forwarding rules to collect sensitive information.

techniques.name: Clipboard Data
techniques.description: Adversaries may collect data stored in the clipboard from users copying information within or between applications.

techniques.name: Automated Collection
techniques.description: Once established within a system or network, an adversary may use automated techniques for collecting internal data.

techniques.name: Peripheral Device Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to gather information about attached peripheral devices and components connected to a computer system.

techniques.name: Audio Capture
techniques.description: An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., microphones and webcams) or applications (e.g., voice and video call services) to capture audio recordings for the purpose of listening into sensitive conversations to gather information.

techniques.name: System Time Discovery
techniques.description: An adversary may gather the system time and/or time zone settings from a local or remote system.

techniques.name: Video Capture
techniques.description: An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., integrated cameras or webcams) or applications (e.g., video call services) to capture video recordings for the purpose of gathering information.

techniques.name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
techniques.description: Adversaries may take advantage of trusted developer utilities to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: MSBuild
techniques.description: Adversaries may use MSBuild to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: ClickOnce
techniques.description: Adversaries may use ClickOnce applications (.appref-ms and .application files) to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: JamPlus
techniques.description: Adversaries may use `JamPlus` to proxy the execution of a malicious script.

techniques.name: Shared Modules
techniques.description: Adversaries may execute malicious payloads via loading shared modules.

techniques.name: Data Encoding
techniques.description: Adversaries may encode data to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

techniques.name: Standard Encoding
techniques.description: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

techniques.name: Non-Standard Encoding
techniques.description: Adversaries may encode data with a non-standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

techniques.name: External Remote Services
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services to initially access and/or persist within a network.

techniques.name: Access Token Manipulation
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify access tokens to operate under a different user or system security context to perform actions and bypass access controls.

techniques.name: Token Impersonation/Theft
techniques.description: Adversaries may duplicate then impersonate another user's existing token to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

techniques.name: Create Process with Token
techniques.description: Adversaries may create a new process with an existing token to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

techniques.name: Make and Impersonate Token
techniques.description: Adversaries may make new tokens and impersonate users to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

techniques.name: Parent PID Spoofing
techniques.description: Adversaries may spoof the parent process identifier (PPID) of a new process to evade process-monitoring defenses or to elevate privileges.

techniques.name: SID-History Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may use SID-History Injection to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

techniques.name: Network Share Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may look for folders and drives shared on remote systems as a means of identifying sources of information to gather as a precursor for Collection and to identify potential systems of interest for Lateral Movement.

techniques.name: Create Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Local Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may create a local account to maintain access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Domain Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may create a domain account to maintain access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Cloud Account
techniques.description: Adversaries may create a cloud account to maintain access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Office Application Startup

techniques.name: Office Template Macros
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

techniques.name: Office Test

techniques.name: Outlook Forms

techniques.name: Outlook Home Page
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

techniques.name: Outlook Rules
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook rules to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

techniques.name: Add-ins

techniques.name: Software Extensions

techniques.name: Browser Extensions

techniques.name: IDE Extensions
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse an integrated development environment (IDE) extension to establish persistent access to victim systems.

techniques.name: Browser Session Hijacking
techniques.description: Adversaries may take advantage of security vulnerabilities and inherent functionality in browser software to change content, modify user-behaviors, and intercept information as part of various browser session hijacking techniques.

techniques.name: Forced Authentication
techniques.description: Adversaries may gather credential material by invoking or forcing a user to automatically provide authentication information through a mechanism in which they can intercept.

techniques.name: Drive-by Compromise
techniques.description: Adversaries may gain access to a system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing.

techniques.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network.

techniques.name: Supply Chain Compromise

techniques.name: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools

techniques.name: Compromise Software Supply Chain

techniques.name: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
techniques.description: Adversaries may manipulate hardware components in products prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

techniques.name: BITS Jobs

techniques.name: Trusted Relationship
techniques.description: Adversaries may breach or otherwise leverage organizations who have access to intended victims.

techniques.name: Hardware Additions

techniques.name: Password Policy Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access detailed information about the password policy used within an enterprise network or cloud environment.

techniques.name: Indirect Command Execution

techniques.name: Malicious File

techniques.name: Malicious Copy and Paste

techniques.name: Malicious Library
techniques.description: Adversaries may rely on a user installing a malicious library to facilitate execution.

techniques.name: Traffic Signaling
techniques.description: Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control.

techniques.name: Port Knocking

techniques.name: Socket Filters

techniques.name: Exploitation for Stealth
techniques.description: Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities to evade detection by hiding activity, suppressing logging, or operating within trusted or unmonitored components.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Credential Access

techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage information repositories to mine valuable information.

techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage the SharePoint repository as a source to mine valuable information.

techniques.name: Code Repositories

techniques.name: Customer Relationship Management Software

techniques.name: Messaging Applications

techniques.name: Databases

techniques.description: Adversaries may use trusted scripts, often signed with certificates, to proxy the execution of malicious files.

techniques.name: PubPrn

techniques.name: SyncAppvPublishingServer

techniques.name: Browser Information Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may enumerate information about browsers to learn more about compromised environments.

techniques.name: System Binary Proxy Execution
techniques.description: Adversaries may bypass process and/or signature-based defenses by proxying execution of malicious content with signed, or otherwise trusted, binaries.

techniques.name: Compiled HTML File
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Compiled HTML files (.chm) to conceal malicious code.

techniques.name: Control Panel
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: CMSTP
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse CMSTP to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: InstallUtil
techniques.description: Adversaries may use InstallUtil to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Mshta
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse mshta.exe to proxy execution of malicious .hta files and Javascript or VBScript through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Msiexec
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse msiexec.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: Odbcconf
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse odbcconf.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads.

techniques.name: Regsvcs/Regasm
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Regsvcs and Regasm to proxy execution of code through a trusted Windows utility.

techniques.name: Regsvr32
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Regsvr32.exe to proxy execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Rundll32

techniques.name: Verclsid

techniques.name: MMC
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse mmc.exe to proxy execution of malicious .msc files.

techniques.name: Electron Applications
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse components of the Electron framework to execute malicious code.

techniques.name: Remote Access Tools
techniques.description: An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network.

techniques.name: IDE Tunneling
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse Integrated Development Environment (IDE) software with remote development features to establish an interactive command and control channel on target systems within a network.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Software
techniques.description: An adversary may use legitimate desktop support software to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

techniques.name: Remote Access Hardware
techniques.description: An adversary may use legitimate remote access hardware to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

techniques.name: XSL Script Processing
techniques.description: Adversaries may bypass application control and obscure execution of code by embedding scripts inside XSL files.

techniques.name: Template Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may create or modify references in user document templates to conceal malicious code or force authentication attempts.

techniques.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Windows Permissions
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Linux and Mac Permissions
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

techniques.name: Execution Guardrails
techniques.description: Adversaries may use execution guardrails to constrain execution or actions based on adversary supplied and environment specific conditions that are expected to be present on the target.

techniques.name: Environmental Keying
techniques.description: Adversaries may environmentally key payloads or other features of malware to evade defenses and constraint execution to a specific target environment.

techniques.name: Mutual Exclusion
techniques.description: Adversaries may constrain execution or actions based on the presence of a mutex associated with malware.

techniques.name: Domain Trust Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to gather information on domain trust relationships that may be used to identify lateral movement opportunities in Windows multi-domain/forest environments.

techniques.name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify the configuration settings of a domain or identity tenant to evade defenses and/or escalate privileges in centrally managed environments.

techniques.name: Group Policy Modification
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to subvert the intended discretionary access controls for a domain, usually with the intention of escalating privileges on the domain.

techniques.name: Trust Modification
techniques.description: Adversaries may add new domain trusts, modify the properties of existing domain trusts, or otherwise change the configuration of trust relationships between domains and tenants to evade defenses and/or elevate privileges.Trust details, such as whether or not user identities are federated, allow authentication and authorization properties to apply between domains or tenants for the purpose of accessing shared resources.

techniques.name: Data Destruction
techniques.description: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.

techniques.name: Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion
techniques.description: Adversaries may modify the lifecycle policies of a cloud storage bucket to destroy all objects stored within.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
techniques.description: Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

techniques.name: Service Stop

techniques.name: Inhibit System Recovery

techniques.name: Defacement

techniques.name: External Defacement
techniques.description: An adversary may deface systems external to an organization in an attempt to deliver messaging, intimidate, or otherwise mislead an organization or users.

techniques.name: Firmware Corruption

techniques.name: Compute Hijacking

techniques.name: Bandwidth Hijacking

techniques.name: SMS Pumping

techniques.name: Cloud Service Hijacking

techniques.name: System Checks
techniques.description: Adversaries may employ various system checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments.

techniques.name: User Activity Based Checks

techniques.name: Time Based Checks

techniques.name: Cloud Service Discovery

techniques.name: Data from Cloud Storage

techniques.description: Adversaries may interrupt availability of system and network resources by inhibiting access to accounts utilized by legitimate users.

techniques.name: Log Enumeration

techniques.name: Content Injection

techniques.name: Hide Infrastructure

techniques.name: Modify Cloud Resource Hierarchy

techniques.name: Email Bombing

techniques.name: Cloud Application Integration

techniques.name: Input Injection

techniques.name: Poisoned Pipeline Execution

techniques.name: Delay Execution

techniques.name: Local Storage Discovery

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Tools

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
techniques.description: An adversary may disable or modify cloud logging capabilities and integrations to limit what data is collected on their activities and avoid detection.

techniques.name: Modify or Spoof Tool UI
techniques.description: Adversaries may spoof or manipulate security tool user interfaces (UIs) to falsely indicate tools are functioning normally and delay detection and response.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log
techniques.description: Adversaries may disable or modify the Linux Audit system to hide malicious activity and avoid detection.

techniques.name: Clear Windows Event Logs
techniques.description: Adversaries may clear Windows Event Logs to hide the activity of an intrusion.

techniques.name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
techniques.description: Adversaries may clear system logs to hide evidence of an intrusion.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify System Firewall
techniques.description: Adversaries may disable or modify host-based or network firewalls to impair defensive mechanisms and enable further action.

techniques.name: Cloud Firewall
techniques.description: Adversaries may disable or modify a firewall within a cloud environment to bypass controls that limit access to cloud resources.

techniques.name: Network Device Firewall
techniques.description: Adversaries may disable network device-based firewall mechanisms entirely or add, delete, or modify particular rules in order to bypass controls limiting network usage.

techniques.name: Windows Host Firewall
techniques.description: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows host firewall to bypass controls limiting network usage.

techniques.name: Safe Mode Boot

techniques.description: Adversaries may input malicious prompts directly into an LLM’s user interface.

mitigations.name: Application Developer Guidance
mitigations.description: Application Developer Guidance focuses on providing developers with the knowledge, tools, and best practices needed to write secure code, reduce vulnerabilities, and implement secure design principles.

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.description: Implement robust Active Directory (AD) configurations using group policies to secure user accounts, control access, and minimize the attack surface.

mitigations.name: Vulnerability Scanning
mitigations.description: Vulnerability scanning involves the automated or manual assessment of systems, applications, and networks to identify misconfigurations, unpatched software, or other security weaknesses.

mitigations.name: User Training
mitigations.description: User Training involves educating employees and contractors on recognizing, reporting, and preventing cyber threats that rely on human interaction, such as phishing, social engineering, and other manipulative techniques.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.description: User Account Management involves implementing and enforcing policies for the lifecycle of user accounts, including creation, modification, and deactivation.

mitigations.name: Threat Intelligence Program
mitigations.description: A Threat Intelligence Program enables organizations to proactively identify, analyze, and act on cyber threats by leveraging internal and external data sources.

mitigations.name: SSL/TLS Inspection
mitigations.description: SSL/TLS inspection involves decrypting encrypted network traffic to examine its content for signs of malicious activity.

mitigations.name: Restrict Web-Based Content
mitigations.description: Restricting web-based content involves enforcing policies and technologies that limit access to potentially malicious websites, unsafe downloads, and unauthorized browser behaviors.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.description: Restricting file and directory permissions involves setting access controls at the file system level to limit which users, groups, or processes can read, write, or execute files.

mitigations.name: Restrict Registry Permissions
mitigations.description: Restricting registry permissions involves configuring access control settings for sensitive registry keys and hives to ensure that only authorized users or processes can make modifications.

mitigations.name: Privileged Process Integrity
mitigations.description: Privileged Process Integrity focuses on defending highly privileged processes (e.g., system services, antivirus, or authentication processes) from tampering, injection, or compromise by adversaries.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.description: Privileged Account Management focuses on implementing policies, controls, and tools to securely manage privileged accounts (e.g., SYSTEM, root, or administrative accounts).

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.description: Set and enforce secure password policies for accounts to reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access.

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.description: Operating System Configuration involves adjusting system settings and hardening the default configurations of an operating system (OS) to mitigate adversary exploitation and prevent abuse of system functionality.

mitigations.name: Remote Data Storage
mitigations.description: Remote Data Storage focuses on moving critical data, such as security logs and sensitive files, to secure, off-host locations to minimize unauthorized access, tampering, or destruction by adversaries.

mitigations.name: Network Segmentation
mitigations.description: Network segmentation involves dividing a network into smaller, isolated segments to control and limit the flow of traffic between devices, systems, and applications.

mitigations.name: Network Intrusion Prevention
mitigations.description: Use intrusion detection signatures to block traffic at network boundaries.

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.description: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) enhances security by requiring users to provide at least two forms of verification to prove their identity before granting access.

mitigations.name: Limit Software Installation
mitigations.description: Prevent users or groups from installing unauthorized or unapproved software to reduce the risk of introducing malicious or vulnerable applications.

mitigations.name: Limit Hardware Installation
mitigations.description: Prevent unauthorized users or groups from installing or using hardware, such as external drives, peripheral devices, or unapproved internal hardware components, by enforcing hardware usage policies and technical controls.

mitigations.name: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
mitigations.description: Restrict access to network resources, such as file shares, remote systems, and services, to only those users, accounts, or systems with a legitimate business requirement.

mitigations.name: Account Use Policies
mitigations.description: Account Use Policies help mitigate unauthorized access by configuring and enforcing rules that govern how and when accounts can be used.

mitigations.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigations.description: Employ network appliances and endpoint software to filter ingress, egress, and lateral network traffic.

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.description: Prevent the execution of unauthorized or malicious code on systems by implementing application control, script blocking, and other execution prevention mechanisms.

mitigations.name: Environment Variable Permissions
mitigations.description: Restrict the modification of environment variables to authorized users and processes by enforcing strict permissions and policies.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.description: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint refers to the use of technologies and strategies to detect and block potentially malicious activities by analyzing the behavior of processes, files, API calls, and other endpoint events.

mitigations.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
mitigations.description: Protect sensitive information at rest, in transit, and during processing by using strong encryption algorithms.

mitigations.name: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
mitigations.description: Disable or remove unnecessary and potentially vulnerable software, features, or services to reduce the attack surface and prevent abuse by adversaries.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.description: Credential Access Protection focuses on implementing measures to prevent adversaries from obtaining credentials, such as passwords, hashes, tokens, or keys, that could be used for unauthorized access.

mitigations.name: Restrict Library Loading
mitigations.description: Restricting library loading involves implementing security controls to ensure that only trusted and verified libraries (DLLs, shared objects, etc.) are loaded into processes.

mitigations.name: Code Signing
mitigations.description: Code Signing is a security process that ensures the authenticity and integrity of software by digitally signing executables, scripts, and other code artifacts.

mitigations.name: Boot Integrity
mitigations.description: Boot Integrity ensures that a system starts securely by verifying the integrity of its boot process, operating system, and associated components.

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.description: Auditing is the process of recording activity and systematically reviewing and analyzing the activity and system configurations.

mitigations.name: Application Isolation and Sandboxing
mitigations.description: Application Isolation and Sandboxing refers to the technique of restricting the execution of code to a controlled and isolated environment (e.g., a virtual environment, container, or sandbox).

mitigations.name: Antivirus/Antimalware
mitigations.description: Antivirus/Antimalware solutions utilize signatures, heuristics, and behavioral analysis to detect, block, and remediate malicious software, including viruses, trojans, ransomware, and spyware.

mitigations.name: Exploit Protection
mitigations.description: Deploy capabilities that detect, block, and mitigate conditions indicative of software exploits.

mitigations.name: Update Software
mitigations.description: Software updates ensure systems are protected against known vulnerabilities by applying patches and upgrades provided by vendors.

mitigations.name: User Account Control
mitigations.description: User Account Control (UAC) is a security feature in Microsoft Windows that prevents unauthorized changes to the operating system.

mitigations.name: Data Backup
mitigations.description: Data Backup involves taking and securely storing backups of data from end-user systems and critical servers.

mitigations.name: Software Configuration
mitigations.description: Software configuration refers to making security-focused adjustments to the settings of applications, middleware, databases, or other software to mitigate potential threats.

mitigations.name: Do Not Mitigate
mitigations.description: The Do Not Mitigate category highlights scenarios where attempting to mitigate a specific technique may inadvertently increase the organization's security risk or operational instability.

mitigations.name: Pre-compromise
mitigations.description: Pre-compromise mitigations involve proactive measures and defenses implemented to prevent adversaries from successfully identifying and exploiting weaknesses during the Reconnaissance and Resource Development phases of an attack.

mitigations.name: Data Loss Prevention
mitigations.description: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) involves implementing strategies and technologies to identify, categorize, monitor, and control the movement of sensitive data within an organization.

mitigations.name: Out-of-Band Communications Channel
mitigations.description: Establish secure out-of-band communication channels to ensure the continuity of critical communications during security incidents, data integrity attacks, or in-network communication failures.
